scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Accelerating Beat of the Fatele
This is Fatele. 19th century.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The fatele originated as a traditional dance-song in Tuvalu.
It faced suppression in the 1860s due to missionary influence but evolved in the 20th century, incorporating elements of the Samoan siva dance.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Performed at weddings, church festivals, and to honor prominent visitors.
It is a competitive tradition that serves as a community celebration.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Traditionally performed sitting or kneeling by women.
Modern performances feature women standing in lines, enacting stories through arm and body movements while men provide rhythmic accompaniment.
on_screen: Formation: Women in lines, men sitting facing them
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music features singing led by older men in a meeting hall (maneapa).
Percussion is provided by beating hands on mats, empty cabin cracker cans, or wooden tea chests.
Listen for the empty cabin cracker cans, wooden boxes, tea chests.
A vocal-heavy performance that starts with a steady, rhythmic pulse on wooden boxes and cans, gradually increasing in volume and speed until an abrupt finish.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned
Waveform or rhythm-pattern graphic: Gradually repeating and quickening

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear titi fakamanumanu (coconut leaf skirts), titi kaulama (layered skirts), teuga saka (tops), and various floral garlands and bands.
Performances occur in community spaces like the maneapa.
